noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: know the qualitative test for a C=C double bond using bromine or bromine water

primer.text: One reagent separates saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons in seconds. Bromine water holds a stubborn orange colour until a double bond attacks it; alkanes leave it untouched. This note runs the test, names the dibromo product that steals the colour, and flags the dark-conditions caveat that keeps the result honest.

lessons.title: Bromine water as the C=C detector
lessons.opening: One reagent answers a whole-class question in seconds: does this hydrocarbon hold a double bond? Orange bromine water keeps its colour against alkanes but bleaches the moment an unsaturated compound opens the Br-Br bond and swallows both atoms across the C=C.
keyPoints: Bromine water is the qualitative test for a carbon-carbon double bond.
An unsaturated compound decolourises orange bromine water by an addition reaction.
The colour loss happens because the Br-Br bond breaks and both bromine atoms join the molecule.
A saturated compound such as an alkane leaves the orange colour unchanged in the dark.
Testing alkanes versus alkenes side by side makes the contrast the answer itself.

low.restatement: Shake the sample with orange bromine water: colour gone means a C=C bond took the bromine in; colour staying means the hydrocarbon is saturated.
low.analogy: The orange dye is a bouncer who only leaves the doorway when a double bond invites both bromine atoms inside.
low.examPointer: Quote the observation (orange to colourless), the reaction type (addition) and the product class (dibromo compound) - three marks live in those three phrases.

medium.restatement: The pi bond polarises and attacks the Br-Br bond, so the reagent is consumed rather than substituted: with alkanes in the dark nothing reacts, while sunlight on an alkane would trigger slow radical substitution and false positives.
medium.analogy: Only one guest gets the door opened for them: the alkene. An alkane with a sunlamp is the impostor case the exam loves to test.
medium.examPointer: If the question mentions sunlight, split your answer: alkene reacts regardless of light; alkane reacts only slowly by radical substitution under UV, so run the comparison in the dark.

check.stem: What observation shows a hydrocarbon is unsaturated in the bromine water test?

options.explanation: The double bond consumes the bromine by addition.
No reaction deepens the reagent's colour.
Nothing precipitates in this test.
The addition consumes both reagents into one product.

check.stem: Which reaction type consumes bromine water with an alkene?

options.explanation: Both bromine atoms join the molecule at the C=C.
Substitution is the alkane's slow UV reaction.
That is the manganate(VII) chemistry.
No acid-base pair operates here.

check.stem: Hexane and hexene are shaken separately with bromine water in the dark. What happens?

options.text: Hexane keeps the orange colour; hexene decolourises it
options.explanation: Saturated hexane cannot open the Br-Br bond without UV help.
Hexane is saturated - it leaves the colour alone in the dark.
Hexene's pi bond attacks the bromine readily.
The outcome is exactly reversed.

check.stem: Why must the alkane comparison be performed in the dark?

options.text: Sunlight enables slow radical substitution of alkanes with bromine, faking a positive
options.explanation: UV light initiates the radical route that bleaches bromine.
Evaporation does not decolourise the reagent.
Alkenes react with bromine water without light.
The reagent is stable without light; the caveat targets the alkane side.

check.stem: What organic product forms when ethene reacts with bromine water?

options.explanation: One bromine lands on each alkene carbon.
That is the HBr addition product - the second bromine must appear.
Bromine brings no oxygen.
That is the manganate oxidation product.

check.stem: State the reagent and the observation used to test for a C=C double bond.
check.modelAnswer: Shake the sample with orange bromine water; decolourisation shows an unsaturated C=C bond is present.

check.stem: Explain, in one sentence each, why the bromine colour disappears with an alkene but not with an alkane in the dark.
check.modelAnswer: The alkene's pi bond opens the Br-Br bond and takes both atoms in by addition; the saturated alkane offers no reactive site, so the reagent survives unchanged.

check.stem: Explain why bromine water is described as testing saturation rather than testing alkenes specifically.
check.modelAnswer: Any unsaturated hydrocarbon - alkene or cycloalkene - consumes the reagent, while any saturated one survives it, so the test distinguishes the saturation classes rather than one named family.

check.stem: A colourless liquid X decolourises bromine water in the dark within seconds. State what bond X must contain and name the reaction type you witnessed.
check.modelAnswer: X must hold a carbon-carbon double bond, and the colour loss was an addition reaction that consumed the bromine across that bond.

glossary.definition: The orange aqueous bromine reagent used as the qualitative test for carbon-carbon double bonds.
Describing a hydrocarbon with only single bonds, which leaves bromine water orange in the dark.
A laboratory observation that identifies a structural feature without measuring a quantity.
